h1:
Pla Som Mahachanachai
Yasothon's Famous Fermented Fish
intro: Ask anyone here about Yasothon's food souvenirs and they'll say pla som before anything else, especially the long-established makers along the Chi River basin around Mahachanachai district. Barb is fermented until it picks up a soft, mellow sourness, then fried crisp on the outside and tender inside and eaten with a plate of hot rice. It's the simple meal Isan folks miss when they're away. We've pulled together the shops that are actually open, how to pick a good batch, how to fry it well, and where to buy it, all in one place.

blocks.html: Pla som is fish fermented with steamed sticky rice, salt, and garlic, then left to develop its sour flavor naturally. It's a food-preservation tradition Isan people have kept alive along the Chi River for generations. Yasothon is especially known for it, above all the pla som made from barb, which has firm flesh and just the right amount of sourness, never so sharp that it turns bitter.

A lot of people assume all of Yasothon's pla som comes from Mahachanachai district. In reality, several of the famous shops are right in Yasothon town, but the province's pla som tradition is tied to the Chi River that runs through Mahachanachai, so the name stuck. We'll tell it straight and cover both the shops in town and the good stuff on the Mahachanachai side together.

blocks.text: What makes Mahachanachai pla som good

blocks.html: The appeal of good pla som comes down to how fresh the starting fish is and getting the fermentation just right. The old-school shops pick good-sized barb, scale them, rinse them clean through several changes of water, rub them with sea salt, then mix in steamed sticky rice and pounded garlic. They ferment for about two days to get a soft sourness while the flesh stays firm and doesn't fall apart, so it smells great and is easy to keep eating once fried.

items: Barb flesh — firm, with a natural sweetness from the fish; the grade Yasothon locals like best
Mellow sourness — it comes from fermenting the sticky rice, not from added acid, so the tang is soft and doesn't bite
That aroma when it fries — the garlic and fermented rice give off a fragrance Isan people know well
Options to choose from — whole pla som, boneless pla som, and minced pla som (fak); pick whatever suits you

blocks.text: Top pla som shops in Yasothon

blocks.html: These are shops that are genuinely open and where locals and travelers stop to buy often, ordered by how well known they are and how easy they are to pop into. Prices are rough ranges that depend on the type of fish and the size, so check at the shop or its page again before you go.

items.name: Mae Yom Pla Som
items.blurb: An old-timer with a traditional recipe in Yasothon town that's been making and selling pla som for decades. They use fresh, hand-picked large barb and ferment every step themselves. It's the first name that comes to mind when people talk about Yasothon pla som. Around Songkran and the Rocket Festival, advance orders pile up fast. They ship nationwide.
items.meta: Khuean Thani Rd, Nai Mueang, Mueang Yasothon · about ฿120/kg

items.name: Ban Mae Koi Pla Som
items.blurb: A shop in town with plenty to choose from: boneless pla som, barb, striped catfish, small and large. They have versions with and without horseshoe crab, and they open early at six. Handy for grabbing some before you carry on.

items.name: Je Pen Pla Som (the old shop)
items.blurb: A long-running pla som shop in Yasothon's old market area, well known to locals. The fish is firm-fleshed with just-right fermentation, and it's easy to drop by since it's in the market, so you can carry on shopping for other souvenirs right after.

items.name: Mae Noi Pla Som Yasothon
items.blurb: A shop on Si Sunthon Road in town that sells house-fermented pla som in several sizes. It's another spot Yasothon locals buy from regularly, good to stop at as you come into town.

items.name: OTOP Pla Som Mahachanachai
items.blurb: Over on the Mahachanachai side, homemaker groups and community shops make pla som as an OTOP product, true to the Chi River way of life, at friendly prices. Good for anyone driving the Mahachanachai route who wants it from the source. Ask around the district market.

items.name: Roadside souvenir stalls on the route into Yasothon
items.blurb: Along the main roads into Yasothon town you'll find several stalls and souvenir shops selling pla som, convenient if you're driving through. Easy to buy, but pick a stall where the fish looks fresh and there's steady turnover of customers.
items.meta: Roadside on the highway into town · prices vary by shop

blocks.title: How to pick a good batch of pla som
blocks.html: Look for firm flesh and a nice color that isn't dull, with a fragrant sour smell rather than a sharp, pungent one. If you're eating it soon, choose a batch that's fully fermented; if you want to keep it for several days, tell the shop you'd like it lightly fermented and keep it chilled.

blocks.text: How to fry pla som and eat it with rice

blocks.html: The easiest and most popular way to eat it is fried. The sour pla som meeting the crispness from frying works really well, and one plate with hot rice is enough to fill you up.

items: Heat the oil to medium, not too hot, since pla som has sugar from the fermented rice and burns easily
Fry until golden and crisp on both sides while the inside stays tender; no need to fry so long it dries out
Eat it with hot rice, sliced shallots, fresh chilies, and fresh vegetables like cucumber or sawtooth coriander to cut the richness
For more of a kick, squeeze on a little lime, or dip it in chili fish sauce to go along with it

blocks.html: Beyond frying, pla som works in plenty of other dishes too: pla som salad (yam), dressed-up pla som, or take the minced pla som (fak) and mix it into beaten egg for a pla som omelet. It's an ingredient you can build several meals around with ease.

blocks.text: Buying it as a souvenir and keeping it fresh

blocks.html: Pla som makes a souvenir people love because it's hard to find outside the area, but it's a fresh fermented product, so you'll want to mind the storage a little to avoid spoiling it.

items.name: Vacuum-sealed bags
items.blurb: Most shops will vacuum-seal it for you, which keeps it clean to carry and pass along and holds the smell in better.

items.name: Chill it right away
items.blurb: Once you're home, the regular fridge compartment keeps it for several days; if you want it to last a week, put it in the freezer.

items.name: Choose lightly fermented
items.blurb: If you have a long way to travel or you're mailing it, ask the shop for a lightly fermented batch so the sourness builds gradually and is just right on arrival.

blocks.title: Order ahead during festival season
blocks.html: Songkran and the Rocket Festival (in May) are peak season for Yasothon pla som. Many of the well-known shops have long queues and sell out fast, so if you have your heart set on a particular one, calling or messaging their page to reserve ahead is the safer bet.

blocks.text: Planning a stop while traveling around Yasothon

blocks.html: If you're visiting Yasothon, grabbing some pla som is easy because the famous shops are right in town, near the old quarter and the market, so you can carry on buying other souvenirs in the same trip. Anyone driving the Mahachanachai route can also look for it from the source on the Chi River side.

faq.q: Which pla som shop in Yasothon is the famous one?
faq.a: The first name that comes to mind is Mae Yom Pla Som, a traditional recipe in town. Next are Ban Mae Koi Pla Som, which has lots to choose from, Je Pen Pla Som (the old shop) in the old market area, and Mae Noi Pla Som on Si Sunthon Road. Over on the Mahachanachai side, there's OTOP pla som made by community groups along the Chi River.

faq.q: What fish is Mahachanachai pla som made from?
faq.a: Most of it is made from barb, which has firm flesh and a natural sweetness, the grade Yasothon locals like best. Some shops also offer striped catfish or boneless pla som to choose from.

faq.q: How much does Yasothon pla som cost?
faq.a: Prices depend on the type of fish and the size. Barb pla som runs about ฿120 per kilogram, while shops that sell by the item, like Ban Mae Koi, fall in the ฿101–250 per item range. Check at the shop or its page again before buying.

faq.q: How do you eat pla som so it tastes good?
faq.a: People usually fry it until golden and crisp and eat it with hot rice, sliced shallots, fresh chilies, and fresh vegetables to cut the richness. It's also good as pla som salad (yam), dressed-up pla som, or a pla som omelet.

faq.q: Can you keep pla som for long after buying it to take home?
faq.a: Pla som is a fresh fermented product, so chill it as soon as you get home. The regular fridge compartment keeps it for several days; for a week, use the freezer. Most shops vacuum-seal it for you, and if you have a long way to travel, asking for a lightly fermented batch is better.
